context: area network · PE mains and services; pressure test, purging and gas-in by the licensed operator

brief.intro: New to this project type? A gas distribution network brings natural gas from a pressure-reducing station to buildings through buried mains — polyethylene (PE) pipe in the streets, steel for the higher-pressure feeders — with a service pipe, a regulator and a meter at each customer. The pipe laying is quick: PE comes in coils or long lengths and is fused together. What sets this network apart is safety. Only qualified welders and fusion operators may make joints, every joint is recorded, the network is pressure-tested, and the moment gas is let in (gas-in) is done by the licensed gas company under its own procedure, after it has inspected everything. Gas keeps its distance from other utilities, especially power cables.

must_get_right: Qualified fusion operators and welders are the controlling resource; every joint is traceable. Plan output per fusion team, not per excavator.
Respect the separation from power cables and other utilities when the corridor is coordinated — gas cannot simply be squeezed into the space left over.
The pressure-reducing station (skid, civil works, upstream connection) is the long-lead item; no section can receive gas before it is commissioned.
Gas-in is done by the gas company after its inspection and a passed test; show the inspection, the test witness and gas-in as dated milestones.

basis_of_planning.standard: AACE Recommended Practice 38R-06 — Documenting the Schedule Basis

sections.heading: Scheduling method & tools
sections.body: A Critical Path Method (CPM) network built in Primavera P6, developed to a Level 3 control schedule with retained-logic progress. Activities are organised by network sector (a valved section that can be tested and gassed on its own) with the PRS and feeder main as common works.

sections.heading: Calendars & working time
sections.body: Standard site calendar. Witnessed tests, inspections and gas-in are dated activities on the gas company's calendar.

sections.heading: Sequencing logic & critical path
sections.body: PRS and feeder main → PE mains by sector → services. Each sector: trench → fuse and lay → pressure test → inspection → purge and gas-in. No sector can be gassed before the PRS is commissioned and the upstream connection is made.

sections.heading: Key assumptions
sections.body: The gas company approves the design and attends tests within the assumed notice; the upstream transmission connection is available; road sections are released in the planned order.

sections.heading: Procurement & long-lead items
sections.body: The schedule tracks the following as milestones because they drive the programme:

rows: Steel line pipe with factory coating

sections.heading: Access, resource & site constraints
sections.body: Mandatory separation from power and other services; hot work (steel welding) needs permits; fusion needs clean, dry, wind-protected conditions.

sections.heading: Risks, float & contingency
sections.body: Main risks: late PRS skid, late upstream connection, failed tightness test, shortage of qualified fusion operators, and third-party damage after testing. Contingency is held before the first gas-in.

sections.heading: Schedule levels of detail
sections.body: Reported at Level 1 (milestones) and Level 2 (summary) to the client; controlled at Level 3 by network sector; expanded to Level 4–5 lookahead for the trenching and fusion teams — consistent with AACE 37R-06.
